How much family protection? Draw the funding gap before choosing coverage

Map future household shortfalls, immediate costs and available resources with a present-value curve, a funding waterfall and sensitivity charts.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

The central idea

Start with the household’s obligations and surviving resources. A salary multiple alone cannot explain the amount or duration of the funding need.

01

Begin with the household shortfall

A protection plan asks what the household would need to fund if an income earner died. The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s life-insurance overview describes uses such as replacing income, supporting dependants and paying debts. It also distinguishes coverage types and emphasizes understanding the policy.

The relevant income gap is the difference between future spending and the surviving household’s available income. It is not automatically the deceased person’s gross salary. Employment-related expenses might end, care costs might rise, and the surviving household may have its own earnings or benefits. Estimate those cash flows before entering a shortfall.

The line chart starts with an annual after-tax gap and increases it each year at the selected escalation rate. The default CAD 40,000 first-year shortfall grows at 2% for 20 years. The first payment arrives at the end of year one. A need that begins immediately, varies by life stage or ends earlier requires a different cash-flow schedule.

02

Translate future support into an amount today

Adding future nominal shortfalls gives the total dollars expected to be paid across different dates. Present value asks what amount today could fund those payments if it earned the selected net return. This model discounts the cash flows at an assumed nominal rate after costs and tax.

For first annual gap G, escalation g, discount rate d and n support years, the income amount today is Σ G(1 + g)t−1 ÷ (1 + d)t, summed from t = 1 to n. Immediate costs are then added without discounting. Escalation and discounting are different operations; using a real rate while also inflating the cash flows would mix conventions.

The default 3% net discount rate produces a combined need of CAD 759,067.82, including CAD 50,000 of immediate costs. A discount rate is an assumption about funding the future payments. It is not a guaranteed return available from an investment or an insurance policy. A lower assumed rate increases the amount needed today for the same positive future shortfalls.

03

Read the waterfall without counting resources twice

The waterfall first adds immediate costs and the present value of income support. It then subtracts assets allocated to this need and existing death benefits. Teal steps add needs; gold steps subtract resources. The navy endpoint shows the modeled net gap or surplus.

With CAD 100,000 of allocated assets and CAD 300,000 of existing benefits, the default additional funding gap is CAD 359,067.82. The figure is a planning estimate under the selected assumptions. It does not identify a suitable policy, establish insurability or determine a premium.

Use a consistent treatment for debts. If immediate costs include paying off the mortgage, remove the corresponding mortgage payments from the future spending gap. If assets are assigned here, do not also promise the same dollars to education and retirement. A home or restricted account may not supply cash when the household needs it; this simplified model assumes the entered resources are fully available today.

04

Test the support period and the discount rate together

The grouped bars compare several support periods against the same available resources. A longer period includes more annual shortfalls. The matrix then varies both duration and discount rate, showing the additional gap after resources in each case.

The shading represents amounts, not probabilities. A darker cell is not more likely. A zero cell means the specified resources cover the modeled need in that scenario; it does not establish that the existing coverage has suitable conditions, duration, ownership or beneficiaries.

Different obligations can have different end dates. Childcare may end before education begins; a partner may retire later; an outstanding debt may be repaid along the way. A detailed plan can replace the single smooth income-gap curve with dated cash flows. Keeping those dates visible is more informative than hiding every obligation in one rounded salary multiple.

05

Review the resources as carefully as the need

Check whether employer coverage continues after a job change and whether the benefit amount, policy term and conditions match the period being modeled. Verify settlement timing, access to assets, beneficiary arrangements and tax treatment for the actual contract and household. These are separate from the present-value calculation.

The charts assume a death occurs today and then fund the resulting household shortfalls. They do not apply mortality probabilities, compare expected insurance claims with premiums or value an insurance policy. They also omit underwriting, exclusions, premium affordability and changes in future coverage.

Review the plan when dependants, debts, income, care needs or existing benefits change. Record which expenses are included, which resources are committed, and which assumptions would change the gap most. The result is a documented funding question to resolve with the relevant licensed professionals, rather than a coverage recommendation generated by a chart.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Charts labelled “Official statistics” use the cited observations with their original periods. All other charts are hypothetical scenarios. The worked examples, scenario assumptions, and research checklists are TickerLantern’s own educational analysis; they are not source-reported investment results. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
